questions.q: What does dayofweek() return for a Sunday?
options: 1 — dayofweek() is 1-indexed starting at Sunday, not 0-indexed like Python's datetime.weekday()
0, exactly matching Python's datetime.weekday()
7, since Sunday is treated as the last day
"Sunday" as a text string
questions.explain: This is a real difference from Python's own date handling worth watching for.

questions.q: Why do year(), month(), and dayofweek() require the column to already be a real timestamp type?
options: Because these functions extract parts of an actual date/time value, which only works correctly on a real timestamp column, not a plain string
They work identically on any column type without exception
They only work on integer columns
They automatically cast any column to timestamp internally first
questions.explain: This is exactly why Lesson 48's .cast() matters — get the column to a real timestamp type before using these functions.

questions.q: What does date_format(col, "MMM d, yyyy") produce?
options: A display string like "Jan 15, 2024" — purely for formatting, not for further date math
A new timestamp column with the time zone changed
The number of days since January 1, 1970
An error, since date_format() requires a numeric pattern
questions.explain: Keep the underlying column as a real timestamp for any actual date math — this function is just for display.

questions.q: Why does building real year() and month() columns now matter for Lesson 61?
options: Lesson 61 (Partitioning Output) splits files by date, typically by year and month — exactly the columns built in this lesson
Lesson 61 has no relationship to date functions at all
Because Lesson 61 requires deleting the original timestamp column entirely
year() and month() are only used for display purposes and never referenced again
questions.explain: Getting real year/month values now is what makes that later partitioning possible.
